analysis.overview: ChatGPT leads on both volume and satisfaction, with 147,085 reviews and a 4.47 rating, and its distinctive terms cluster around everyday utility for students and casual users — homework help, editing, and a conversational "friend" framing. Google Gemini occupies a clear mobile-assistant niche, with its praise and complaints both circling the same terms — phone, screen, video, live — suggesting users engage with it primarily as a device-integrated assistant rather than a standalone AI. Perplexity and Claude are the most polarising products, both carrying a 1.60 standard deviation against the field average closer to 1.35, with Perplexity distinctively positioned as a research and sourcing tool whose complaints center on subscription cost and search limits, while Claude's entire keyword footprint — praised for coding and model capability, complained about for usage limits and message caps — marks it as a power-user coding tool bottlenecked by access restrictions. Microsoft Copilot's distinctive terms around Windows, formatting, and keyboard input suggest a productivity and document-editing use case, though its complaints about the enter key and line formatting point to friction in that exact workflow. The clearest competitive split is that ChatGPT owns general consumer use, Gemini owns mobile integration, Perplexity owns research, Claude owns coding, and Copilot targets Office-style productivity — but Claude and Perplexity's low ratings and high polarisation signal that their monetisation models are actively damaging user satisfaction.

products.ChatGPT: ChatGPT stands out strongly as a learning and productivity tool, with its distinctive positive keywords clustering around student use cases — homework, studying, and editing — and users frequently describing it in personal, emotionally close terms like "best friend." The 76.7% five-star rate and positive average sentiment of 0.478 confirm this enthusiasm is widespread, not just vocal. The main pain points centre on accuracy and value: negative keywords like wrong, incorrect, incorrect answers, and information signal that factual reliability is a recurring frustration, while upgrade, plus, and money point to friction around the paywall. Accuracy is effectively a double-edged theme here — it is likely central to why students praise the app when it works, and why they give one star when it does not.
products.Claude: Claude stands out most clearly for its coding capabilities and its tiered model/plan structure, with distinctive positive associations around reasoning quality and task completion across professional use cases like accounting. The 60% five-star rate reflects genuine satisfaction when the product works as expected, but the 19% one-star rate and high polarisation (std dev 1.60) signal a significant minority having a sharply different experience. Usage limits are the single most telling feature: they appear in both the positive and negative distinctive keyword sets, meaning some users appreciate the transparency of the plan structure while a substantial portion of critics find the limits hit too quickly, sometimes within a single message, making the product feel unusable. Negative reviews also flag account-level issues — banning, verification, token caps — suggesting friction around access and trust that compounds the frustration with restrictions.
products.Google_Gemini: Google Gemini is most distinctly associated with device-native functionality — voice assistance, live screen interaction, phone integration, and Android-specific features like music and video — and these are clearly its headline strengths for most users, reflected in a 72.4% five-star rate and an above-midpoint sentiment of 0.44. However, the same features that drive praise also drive its worst reviews: assistant behavior, video, screen, image generation, and loading speed appear in both the top positive and top negative keyword sets, meaning user experience on these capabilities is sharply divided rather than uniformly positive. The 1.35 standard deviation in ratings confirms this polarisation — a substantial 11.6% of reviewers gave one star, and negative reviews specifically call out slowness, loading issues, language handling, and problems with auto and image generation. The positive reviews themselves are notably thin on specifics ("excellent," "best"), which suggests broad satisfaction among fans but little articulated depth, while critics are pointing to concrete functional failures in the product's core differentiating features.
products.Microsoft_Copilot: Microsoft Copilot earns strong overall marks, with 73.5% five-star reviews and a 4.32 average, and its distinctive praise centres on Windows integration and its utility as a direct, accessible resource for navigating tasks and exploring possibilities within that ecosystem. The sentiment score of 0.41 and relatively high polarisation (std dev 1.32) suggest the product works well for many but fails badly for others. The most concentrated pain point is content restriction: negative keywords like copyrighted, restrictions, boundaries, and copy point to users hitting refusals or limitations, while format, line, and keyboard suggest friction with how responses are structured and how input is handled. Notably, "pilot" appears as a distinctive term in both positive and negative reviews, suggesting Copilot's core AI behaviour is both a selling point and a source of frustration — likely around image generation, where negative reviews explicitly describe the feature misreading requests or refusing them as inappropriate.
products.Perplexity: Perplexity stands out most clearly as a research and search tool, with users distinctively praising it for providing cited sources, accurate information, and balanced results — capabilities that set it apart from other AI products in this competitive set. The 63.9% five-star rate and positive sentiment of 0.38 confirm a genuinely satisfied core user base who value it as a cited search engine rather than a generic chatbot. However, the high rating polarisation (std dev 1.60) alongside a 19.2% one-star rate signals a meaningful frustrated minority, and the negative keywords point to friction around the subscription model, free tier search limits, and account or payment entry barriers. Notably, "research" and "computer" appear in both positive and negative keyword sets, suggesting that while power users praise its research depth, others hit walls — likely free-tier search caps or upload restrictions — that undercut that same core use case.
